lessons.title: Fronts
lessons.objective: You can tell a 4-3 from a 3-4 and say who rushes.

payload.prompt: What is the main difference between a 4-3 and a 3-4 front?

options.text: The 4-3 has four linemen and three linebackers; the 3-4 has three linemen and four linebackers
The 4-3 is more aggressive; the 3-4 is more defensive
The 4-3 is used by bad teams; the 3-4 is used by good teams

explanation.correct: Exactly. A 4-3 puts four big bodies on the line to clog the middle. A 3-4 puts only three on the line and uses a fourth linebacker to rush from the edge.
explanation.incorrect: The numbers tell the story: four linemen versus three. That changes where the pass rush comes from.
explanation.sayThisLine: Four-three is four on the line; three-four is three on the line with four backers.

payload.prompt: Match each front to its job description.

pairs.definition: Four linemen clog the middle; three backers cover underneath and clean up runs.
Three linemen take up blockers; four backers rush the edges and fill gaps.
Rushes the passer from the edge; can be as important as a defensive end.

explanation.summary: Each front trades numbers on the line for numbers in the backfield. Both are common base fronts.
explanation.sayThisLine: Four-three: four on the line. Three-four: four backers.

payload.prompt: Tap where the four defensive linemen line up in a 4-3.

diagram.alt: A football field showing the line of scrimmage with defensive players positioned. Four big players are on the line at the center and shoulder gaps. Three more defenders line up behind them.

explanation.correct: Right. The four linemen take up space right on the line. The three backers stand about five yards back to read and react.
explanation.incorrect: The four linemen line up directly on or very close to the line of scrimmage, taking up blockers.

payload.prompt: In a 3-4, the outside linebackers are expected to rush the quarterback like defensive ends. True or false?

scene.alt: A defensive alignment showing three linemen taking on blockers while two linebackers sprint toward the offense's backfield.

explanation.correct: True. In a 3-4, the outside backers are pass rushers. They have to get off the line fast to pressure the quarterback, not just cover underneath.
explanation.incorrect: Yes, that is exactly what they do. A 3-4 outside linebacker is almost like a defensive end in pass rush responsibility.

payload.prompt: Order these defenders from closest to the line to deepest.

items.why: Linemen start on the line of scrimmage.
Linebackers stand a few yards behind the line.
Safeties start deepest, with the whole field in front of them.

explanation.correct: Yes. The line engages first, the linebackers fill in behind, and the safeties play deepest.
explanation.incorrect: Work from the closest defenders to the deepest: linemen on the line, linebackers a few yards back, safeties deepest.

payload.prompt: In a 3-4, outside linebackers often set the edge against runs. True or false?

scene.alt: A football play showing an offensive run play going to the edge, with a 3-4 linebacker charging upfield to crash the gap.

explanation.correct: True. A 3-4 outside linebacker lines up near the edge, so he can force a run back inside or chase it down, as well as rush the passer.
explanation.incorrect: Yes. Outside linebackers in a 3-4 start near the edge, so they are the ones who have to turn a run back inside.

lessons.title: Man or zone
lessons.objective: You can explain the difference between man and zone coverage.

payload.prompt: What is the core difference between man and zone coverage?

options.text: Man coverage: each defender guards a person. Zone coverage: each defender guards an area.
Man coverage is used on first down. Zone coverage is used on third down.
Man coverage is safer. Zone coverage is riskier.

explanation.correct: That is the fundamental split. Man coverage is about following your guy everywhere. Zone is about owning a patch of grass.
explanation.incorrect: The two defenses differ in assignment. In man you follow a receiver. In zone you guard a spot and whoever enters it.

payload.prompt: In man coverage with no safety deep, a corner beaten deep has no help. True or false?

scene.alt: A football field showing a corner following a receiver one-on-one, with the receiver running downfield away from other defenders.

explanation.correct: True. That is the risk of man coverage with no deep safety (Cover 0). If the receiver wins, the quarterback throws deep and the corner is on his own.
explanation.incorrect: Yes. With no safety over the top, a beaten corner has no backup. Many man coverages do keep a safety deep, which is why this gamble is called Cover 0.

payload.prompt: Match each coverage type to what a defender looks for.

pairs.definition: A defender picks a receiver at the snap and stays glued to him no matter where he runs.
A defender covers an area of the field and reacts to any receiver entering his zone.
Watch pre-snap motion: if the corner follows the receiver across the field, it is man. If he stays in place, it is zone.

explanation.summary: Man is reactive to one player. Zone is reactive to the field. They look and feel completely different.
explanation.sayThisLine: Man: follow one guy. Zone: guard your spot.

payload.prompt: Bunch formations can cause traffic for man defenders. True or false?

scene.alt: Multiple receivers bunched to one side against zone defenders spread across the field.

explanation.correct: True. Receivers stacked close together cross paths, and a defender following his man can get caught on a teammate, like a natural pick.
explanation.incorrect: Yes. When receivers run tight, crossing routes, man defenders have to fight through traffic. That is one reason offenses use bunch sets.

payload.prompt: A corner follows a receiver in motion across the formation. What does that suggest?

options.text: Man coverage
Zone coverage
A blitz

explanation.correct: A man defender follows his receiver wherever he goes. It is one of the best pre-snap clues, though a defense can try to hide it.
explanation.incorrect: A zone defender usually stays in his area and passes the receiver along. A corner who travels with the motion is likely in man coverage.

statement.speaker: Coach watching game
statement.text: They are in man coverage today. The receiver shook him off the ball.

payload.question: What just happened?

options.text: The receiver was open and caught the ball
The receiver got away from the defender covering him and created space
The defense switched to zone coverage mid-play
The receiver interfered with the cornerback

payload.translation: In man coverage, when a receiver shakes a defender off the ball, it means the receiver got separation and the defender could not stay with him.

followUps.line: Was that the receiver running a better route or the corner getting beat?
followUps.why: Shows you can assess whether a receiver or cornerback won that play.

followUps.line: Would zone coverage have been better there?
followUps.why: Tests your sense of when each coverage works.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: If unsure, say the defender could not stay with him, then ask whether it was a great route or a beaten corner.

lessons.title: The deep safeties
lessons.objective: You can spot one-high and two-high shells.

payload.prompt: Why does a defense choose between one-high and two-high safeties?

options.text: One-high can bring a safety near the line to stop the run; two-high keeps both safeties deep to cut off big plays
One-high is for sunny days. Two-high for cloudy days.
One-high = man. Two-high = zone.

explanation.correct: It is a trade-off. One deep safety lets the other one help against the run, but it leaves fewer defenders deep. Two deep safeties protect against big passes but leave fewer defenders near the line.
explanation.incorrect: The shell decides where the safeties start. One-high keeps one safety deep and one closer to the line; two-high keeps both deep. One-high is not always man, and two-high is not always zone.

payload.prompt: Tap where a single-high safety lines up before the snap.

diagram.alt: A football field showing offensive and defensive formations with a deep view showing where safeties position themselves.

hotspots.label: One safety deep in the middle

explanation.correct: One-high means one safety deep in the middle of the field, with the whole deep area in front of him.
explanation.incorrect: The single-high safety stands deep in the middle, usually around 12 to 15 yards off the line.

payload.prompt: Match each shell to its strengths and weaknesses.

pairs.definition: One safety deep in the middle; the other can creep toward the line. Helps the run, riskier deep.
Two safeties split the deep field in halves. Better against deep passes, but easier to run against.
It depends on what the offense does well: one-high to crowd the run, two-high to protect against big pass plays.

explanation.summary: The shell is the defense's first choice before the snap, and it hints at what the defense is worried about.
explanation.sayThisLine: One-high helps the run. Two-high protects deep.

payload.prompt: Two-high shells usually leave fewer defenders near the line. True or false?

scene.alt: Two safeties split wide at the top of the screen, both able to attack downhill toward a run play.

explanation.correct: True. With both safeties deep, the defense usually has only six or seven defenders in the box, so running against two-high can be easier.
explanation.incorrect: Yes. Two deep safeties protect against big passes, but it means fewer defenders near the line. That is why offenses like to run against two-high.

payload.prompt: How many defenders are in the box on a stacked (heavy) run look?

explanation.correct: Eight. A normal base look has seven near the line; a safety stepping down makes eight. Six is a light box.
explanation.incorrect: A normal base look has seven defenders in the box. Adding a safety makes eight, a stacked box. Six is a light box.

payload.prompt: Why is a two-high shell easier to run against?

options.text: Only six or seven defenders are near the line
The safeties are slower than usual
Two-high is not allowed on running downs

explanation.correct: With both safeties deep, there are fewer defenders in the box. Offenses often run against two-high to exploit it.
explanation.incorrect: Two-high puts both safeties deep, so fewer defenders are near the line. That is why runs can work against it.

lessons.title: Read the coverage
lessons.objective: You can name the coverage and find the open receiver.

payload.prompt: You are the quarterback and you see a Cover 3 zone (three deep, four underneath). Where is the open window?

options.text: Deep down the sideline because corners are one-on-one
In the seams between the deep thirds because the middle is split wide
Nowhere, because Cover 3 covers every area equally

explanation.correct: In Cover 3, two corners and a safety split the deep field into thirds. A receiver running up the seam between them stretches the one middle safety, who cannot cover both sides.
explanation.incorrect: Cover 3 has three deep defenders for the whole deep field, so the gaps between those thirds, the seams, are the soft spots. Deep sidelines have a corner on them.

payload.prompt: Match each coverage name to what it does.

pairs.definition: Two safeties each take half of the deep field, and the corners sit shallower to cover the flats.
Three defenders split the deep field into thirds, and four cover underneath.
Cover 2 can be hit in the deep middle and deep sidelines. Cover 3 can be stretched in the seams and flats.

explanation.summary: Both are zone coverages. Cover 2 is tight on short routes but has holes deep, while Cover 3 is stronger deep but thinner in the seams and flats.
explanation.sayThisLine: Cover 2 is two deep. Cover 3 is three deep.

payload.prompt: Two safeties deep, each taking a half. Coverage?

options.text: Cover 3, because three deep defenders can split the field
Cover 2, with two safeties each taking a half of the deep field
Man coverage, because corners are on receivers

explanation.correct: It looks like Cover 2: two safeties split the deep field in halves while the corners cover the flats. A defense can disguise it, which is why reading after the snap matters.
explanation.incorrect: Two safeties each taking a deep half is Cover 2. A man look can start in the same alignment, so the coverage is not certain until the play starts.

payload.prompt: In Cover 2, the deep middle between the safeties is a classic soft spot. True or false?

scene.alt: Two safeties split wide showing a gap down the middle seam of the field where a receiver can run.

explanation.correct: True. Two safeties split the deep field in halves, which leaves the middle between them thin. Teams try to cover it with a linebacker dropping deep.
explanation.incorrect: Yes. The two safeties each take a half, so the deep middle is a known weak spot. A receiver up the seam can find room there.

payload.prompt: Four vertical routes against Cover 2. Why does it stress the defense?

options.text: Four deep routes against two deep safeties means someone gets open
Each safety can cover two receivers without trouble
Cover 2 has four deep defenders

explanation.correct: Cover 2 has only two deep defenders. Four receivers running deep put four targets on two safeties, so one of them is likely open.
explanation.incorrect: Cover 2 has two deep defenders, not four, and each safety cannot cover two routes at once. Four vertical routes create more targets than defenders.

payload.prompt: Two safeties deep and split wide. What shell is that?

options.text: Two-high shell (Cover 2 variant)
Zero-high shell (Cover 0)
One-high shell

explanation.correct: Two safeties deep is a two-high shell. Cover 2, Cover 4 and some man calls all start here, so the shell alone does not reveal the coverage.
explanation.incorrect: Count the safeties deep: two is two-high, one is one-high, and none is zero-high (Cover 0).

lessons.title: The pass rush
lessons.objective: You can say what a sack, a hurry and pressure mean.

payload.prompt: Match each pass rush outcome to its definition.

pairs.definition: Tackled the QB behind the line for a loss of yards. Big negative play.
Forces QB to move or throw early, even without a sack. Huge for defense.
Gets close to the QB, making his throw rushed and often inaccurate.

explanation.summary: A sack is the biggest win. Pressure and hurries count too, because they change the throw even without a sack.
explanation.sayThisLine: Sack is a tackle. Pressure is forcing action. Hurry is forcing a bad throw.

payload.prompt: What is the baseline number of pass rushers the defense typically sends?

options.text: Two, so the quarterback always has time
Four (the defensive line), unless they blitz
Six or more, to guarantee a sack

explanation.correct: Four is the base: the four defensive linemen rush while linebackers and defensive backs cover. Anything more is a blitz.
explanation.incorrect: The front four rush. More than four is extra and usually a blitz. Less than four is rare unless it is a prevent defense.

payload.prompt: A stunt swaps lanes to confuse blockers and free up a rusher. True or false?

scene.alt: Two defensive linemen crossing lanes just after the snap, with an offensive lineman left confused about who to block.

explanation.correct: True. A stunt works because the offense assigns blocks pre-snap, then the defense switches post-snap. One rusher gets free.
explanation.incorrect: Yes, stunts are designed to confuse blocking assignments and create unblocked rushers.

statement.speaker: Analyst on broadcast
statement.text: That pass rush was elite today. The line applied constant pressure and got three sacks.

payload.question: What did the pass rush do well?

options.text: It gave up big plays on third down
It got to the quarterback fast and consistently, including three times for a loss of yards
It let the quarterback scramble for short gains
It gave the corners time to cover receivers

payload.translation: An elite pass rush means getting consistent pressure and creating sacks. The defense dominated.

followUps.line: Were the sacks from blitzes or just the front four?
followUps.why: Shows you are thinking about rush package and whether it took risks.

followUps.line: Can the offense adjust to stop the rush next game?
followUps.why: Tests whether you understand that pass protection schemes can change.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: If unsure, ask if the sacks came from the base front four or if the defense had to blitz.

payload.prompt: Against an elite edge rusher, how can the offense help the tackle?

options.text: Help with a blocker or slide protection
Hope the tackle wins one-on-one
Hope the quarterback escapes

explanation.correct: Elite edge rushers win matchups. Chip with a back, tight end, or slide protection to give help. That is how offense accounts for them.
explanation.incorrect: One-on-one against an elite rusher is a losing battle. You need a second blocker or scheme help.

payload.prompt: Tap the spot the pass rushers are trying to reach.

diagram.alt: A football field showing the line of scrimmage with the offensive line and quarterback in his pocket behind it.

explanation.correct: The quarterback is the target. Linemen have to get across the line of scrimmage and into the pocket.
explanation.incorrect: Pass rushers penetrate through the line of scrimmage (the gaps) to reach the quarterback in the pocket.

lessons.title: The blitz
lessons.objective: You can explain the risk and reward of a blitz.

payload.prompt: What defines a blitz?

options.text: Sending more pass rushers than the usual four linemen, often a linebacker or defensive back
A defense that only covers the deep pass and ignores runs
A penalty for hitting the quarterback too hard

explanation.correct: A blitz is aggression. You send extra rushers (five, six, or more) to get after the quarterback faster.
explanation.incorrect: Blitz means more than the usual pass rushers. It is a calculated gamble: more pressure but fewer defenders covering.

payload.prompt: When blitzing, what is the main risk if the QB has time?

options.text: Fewer defenders in coverage, receivers get open
The blitz always fails
Offense calls a penalty

explanation.correct: That is the blitz gamble. More pass rushers means fewer in coverage. If QB has time, receivers are open.
explanation.incorrect: Blitzing sacrifices coverage. More rushing means fewer defending, so open windows if the pressure fails.

payload.prompt: Match each blitz type to what it is.

pairs.definition: A linebacker rushes the quarterback instead of dropping into coverage, leaving that area undefended.
A corner or safety rushes instead of covering deep, risking big plays downfield.
Man coverage with no free safety, usually paired with an all-out blitz. One mistake is a touchdown.

explanation.summary: Blitzes come from anywhere. Cover 0 is the most aggressive: everyone covers a man, and everyone else rushes.
explanation.sayThisLine: Blitz is extra rushers. Cover 0 is man with no help.

payload.prompt: A late hit after the quarterback releases is roughing, even if on a blitz. True or false?

scene.alt: A quarterback releasing a pass while a blitzing linebacker arrives late and hits him.

explanation.correct: True. The blitz does not excuse a late hit. If the quarterback has released the ball, hitting him is roughing the passer regardless of intent.
explanation.incorrect: Yes. A blitz does not excuse a hit after the throw. Defenders have to pull up once the ball is gone.

payload.prompt: In a five-man rush, what percent of the 11 defenders are in coverage?

explanation.correct: Five rushers leave six in coverage. Six of eleven is about 55 percent.
explanation.incorrect: With 11 defenders and five rushing, six are left to cover. That is about 55 percent, so coverage is thinner than on a standard four-man rush.

payload.prompt: Four linemen plus one linebacker rushing equals how many total blitzers?

options.text: Four, so this is base (no blitz)
Five, so this is a one-man blitz
Six or more

explanation.correct: Five total: four linemen on the line plus one linebacker blitzing. That is one extra rusher beyond the base four.
explanation.incorrect: Count the linemen (four) plus the blitzing linebacker (one). That is five total rushers.

lessons.title: Nickel and matchups
lessons.objective: You can say why defenses use five defensive backs.

payload.prompt: Why do defenses use nickel (five defensive backs) on obvious passing downs?

options.text: It guarantees a sack on every passing down
Defensive backs are faster than linebackers, which helps against three and four receiver sets
Five defensive backs always allow blitzing

explanation.correct: On obvious passing downs, the offense usually has extra receivers. A fifth defensive back brings more speed in coverage than a third linebacker would.
explanation.incorrect: Nickel is about matching speed to the pass threat. Corners and safeties are built to cover receivers, and nothing guarantees a sack.

payload.prompt: Match nickel concepts to what they do.

pairs.definition: Five defensive backs (corners and safeties) instead of the usual four. Used on passing downs.
A corner lines up tight on a receiver and jams him at the line to disrupt his route. Aggressive and physical.
A linebacker trying to cover a fast slot receiver, like a chess mismatch. Nickel takes the linebacker out.

explanation.summary: Nickel is speed. Press coverage is aggression. Together they make defenses tough on passing plays.
explanation.sayThisLine: Nickel: five DBs for speed. Press: jam the receiver at the line.

payload.prompt: A nickel defense still has two linebackers on the field. True or false?

scene.alt: A nickel alignment with five defensive backs spread across the field covering five receivers.

explanation.correct: True. Nickel is usually four linemen, two linebackers and five defensive backs. It swaps one linebacker for a defensive back.
explanation.incorrect: Yes. Nickel takes out one linebacker, not all of them, leaving two. The extra defender is a defensive back.

statement.speaker: Analyst
statement.text: The offense has a great slot receiver and on nickel the defense has to get a corner matched up on him.

payload.question: Why does this matter?

options.text: The slot receiver can run more routes from the slot
A corner who is not quick enough can be beaten by the receiver's speed and quickness
The defense will be forced to blitz the slot receiver
It means the offense will score

payload.translation: In nickel, corner matchups matter a lot. A mismatch (fast receiver on a slow corner) is an easy target.

followUps.line: Can the defense move a different corner to cover the slot?
followUps.why: Shows you are thinking about defensive adjustments.

followUps.line: Is the slot receiver faster than the corner?
followUps.why: Tests whether you assess matchups tactically.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: If unsure, ask whether the corner has the speed and cover skills to stay with this receiver.

payload.prompt: Complete this sentence about nickel personnel.
payload.template: A nickel package replaces {{removed}} with an additional {{added}}.

explanation.correct: Nickel takes out a linebacker and puts in a defensive back, often a corner or a safety.
explanation.incorrect: From base to nickel, you remove one linebacker and add one defensive back.

payload.prompt: If a nickel corner plays press and the receiver beats the jam, what is the risk?

options.text: The receiver runs a shorter route
The receiver gets free off the line and may have no help deep
Offensive pass interference is called

explanation.correct: Press coverage is aggressive. If the corner loses the jam and there is no safety help, the receiver can have a big play.
explanation.incorrect: Press is a gamble. Jamming the receiver can wreck his route, but losing the jam leaves the corner chasing.

lessons.title: Cover 4 and Cover 1 and 0
lessons.objective: You can place every coverage on a risk ladder.

payload.prompt: Order these by deep defenders, fewest to most.

items.text: Cover 0: man coverage, no free help
Cover 1: man with one free safety
Cover 2: two safeties split the deep field
Cover 3: three defenders split the deep field
Cover 4 (quarters): four defenders each take a quarter

explanation.correct: Cover 0 has no deep help, Cover 1 has one safety deep, Cover 2 two, Cover 3 three and Cover 4 four. More deep help is safer against big plays but can be thinner underneath.
explanation.incorrect: Count the deep defenders: zero, one, two, three, four. More deep help means more conservative, but fewer defenders near the line.

payload.prompt: Match the named coverages to their definitions.

pairs.definition: Man coverage with zero safeties helping deep. One mistake is a touchdown. Maximum blitz, maximum risk.
Man coverage underneath with one safety deep (single-high). The free safety is the safety net.
Four deep defenders each take a quarter of the field. Tough on deep shots but weak to the intermediate game.

explanation.summary: Cover 0 is aggressive gambling. Cover 1 is moderate. Cover 4 is defensive depth.
explanation.sayThisLine: Cover 0: no help, all-in blitz. Cover 1: one help. Cover 4: four helping.

payload.prompt: What is the main weakness of Cover 4 (quarters) coverage?

options.text: It is weak to deep passes because four defenders split the field
It is weak to intermediate and short routes because all four helpers are split deep and the underneath is thin
It cannot stop the run because all defenders are in coverage

explanation.correct: Cover 4 has four defenders sharing the deep field, so fewer are left underneath. A receiver settling in the zone or running an intermediate route finds grass.
explanation.incorrect: Four defensive help sounds great, but it leaves the middle underneath soft. Seams and short passes thrive.

payload.prompt: Cover 0 usually pairs with a blitz to get sacks fast. True or false?

scene.alt: An all-out defensive blitz with all 11 defenders rushing or in man coverage with no help.

explanation.correct: True. Cover 0 is a kamikaze call. You need sacks or pressure to justify giving up the safety help.
explanation.incorrect: Yes, Cover 0 is so risky that you almost always blitz. The idea is to kill the play before the receiver gets open.

payload.prompt: Against vertical seam routes, which coverage gives more deep help?

options.text: Cover 1 with one safety deep
Cover 4 with four deep helpers
Both are equally good against seams

explanation.correct: Cover 4 divides the deep field, making seams much tougher. One safety (Cover 1) leaves room for seams to fit.
explanation.incorrect: Cover 4 has four defenders helping deep. Cover 1 has only one. Four is better for the deep pass.

payload.prompt: You see corners tight on receivers with no safeties helping deep. What is this coverage?

options.text: Cover 0: man with no safety help
Cover 1: man with one free safety
Cover 4: four helpers in the deep

explanation.correct: Cover 0 puts corners on islands with zero help. Every defender is either covering a man or rushing.
explanation.incorrect: No safeties helping means no free safety. Zero help is Cover 0, the all-in gamble.
